I'm a retired physical chemist. I still mess about with simulations on a free online package — I'll call it BenchMol — for questions that just interest me, since my old university license lapsed. The free tier has a click-through terms of service, the usual forty pages nobody negotiates, but one clause is in plain English:

'You may use the Service solely for your own personal, non-commercial research or educational purposes. You may not use the Service, or any results generated by the Service, in connection with any commercial product or process, or for the benefit of any commercial enterprise.'

Last spring I got curious about a reaction network in a paper, ran a set of calculations purely for my own amusement, and posted a short note on a chemistry blog saying two of the paper's proposed intermediates looked thermodynamically silly. Then an old postdoc of mine, who's now at a startup, emailed to say they'd been looking at the same network for a possible patent and my note had saved them from going down two blind alleys. No money changed hands; I didn't know what they were working on; I have no stake in the company.

Am I in breach? At the moment I ran the calculations, the use was plainly personal and non-commercial, but a result I generated did end up 'for the benefit of a commercial enterprise' in the clause's own words. I care less about the practical answer — I doubt BenchMol is coming after a retiree — than about what it would take for the clause to reach me at all, and whether any coherent reading of it catches genuine commercial exploitation while leaving my sort of case alone. Walk me through what the text, the purpose of the clause, and a reasonable reader would each say. Then give me a definite verdict on which of those interpretations should control here, and whether the click-wrap nature of the thing should make a court or a careful reader lean one way rather than another. If you think the clause does catch me, tell me whether that means it's badly drafted or whether 'for the benefit of' simply has to be read that broadly to be workable.
